items.t: GoPro to be acquired for $285M, will remain a public company
items.d: GoPro is merging with a company that builds AI infrastructure, and will continue supporting existing consumer products.
items.fullText: After years of financial struggles, action camera pioneer GoPro is being acquired for $285 million. A company called Starman Optical has agreed to merge with GoPro. The deal involves Starman Optical paying GoPro shareholders $1.14 per share and leaving those shareholders with about 10% of the newly combined company. The deal, expected to close by the end of this year, will wipe away GoPro’s outstanding debt of $92 million. The merger, announced Tuesday morning, comes a few months after GoPro revealed it was considering pivoting from building cameras to becoming a defense tech company. A day or so ago, YouTuber Markiplier revealed he had amassed an 8.5% stake in GoPro. That appears to still be in the cards, as the company said the merger will “maximize the value of GoPro’s IP and growth potential in consumer, commercial and defense markets by recapitalizing the company, strengthening its balance sheet, investing in growth and onshoring the manufacturing of products for strategic markets.” GoPro will also “fully support” its existing consumer products while “investing in growth and a broader, diversified product roadmap.” It’s not exactly clear what all that means, and Starman Optical doesn’t have a significant track record to judge its performance. The company bills itself as an “optical-photonics company focused on the development and domestic manufacturing of optical transceivers and related photonics technologies through its Starman New Photonics business.” Both Starman Optical and Starman New Photonics are part of Starman Holding, which owns consumer tech brands like Incase, Incipio, and Griffin. items.t: If space data centers feel far-fetched, why not interstellar travel?
items.d: The team behind Starcloud's orbital data centers has a new high-risk space project: Sending a probe to Alpha Centauri.
items.fullText: The founders behind Starcloud , a startup with plans to operate a fleet of GPUs in orbit, have a new pitch for potential investors: a plan to send a tiny spacecraft on an 80,000-year journey to Alpha Centauri. If they do it, it will be the first human-built object explicitly aimed for another star, and the sixth to leave our solar system. Dubbed Fermi Explorer , the non-profit behind the mission emerged today to ask for partners, donations, and advice. The initial team — Starcloud founders Philip Johnston, Adi Oltean, and Ezra Feilden, along with program manager Garret Jameson — has put together a plan to use proven space technologies to send a vehicle with a 10 cm square payload, weighing 1 kilogram, into interstellar space. The founders say they are launching this mission in the spirit of human exploration; to achieve a historical first; and to test the limits of the Fermi paradox , which attempts to explain why we have yet to find other intelligent life in the universe and gives the mission its name. The mission is intended to cost about $15 million and plans to launch in 2029. The non-profit is soliciting vendors to build the vehicle, funding to pay them, and scientific and artistic payloads to send, à la the sensors and Golden Record onboard NASA’s Voyager space probe, the first human spacecraft to leave our solar system. Most plans for interstellar exploration stumble when dealing with the vast distances involved and the comparatively slow methods we have to cross them. Voyager, launched in 1977, is now about 26 billion km from Earth; Alpha Centauri, the nearest star to our solar system, is 41 trillion km away. The last time Silicon Valley took on this challenge, a non-profit called Breakthrough Starshot, founded in 2016 by Yuri Milner and backed by Mark Zuckerberg, envisioned a multibillion-dollar effort to use a novel laser-based propulsion system to reach Alpha Centauri in 20 to 30 years. items.fullText: NVIDIA NVLink Fusion Expands With NVHBM Custom High-Bandwidth Memory Amazon’s Annapurna Labs will be the first to collaborate on NVHBM technology alongside NVLink Fusion. August 26, 2026 by Jesse Clayton 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! The next wave of AI is placing new demands on infrastructure. As AI agents and trillion-parameter workloads become mainstream, the performance of AI infrastructure depends not only on compute, but on how compute, memory, storage, networking and software are designed together as a unified system. To help hyperscalers and AI innovators build the next generation of semi-custom AI infrastructure, NVIDIA today expanded NVIDIA NVLink Fusion with NVIDIA NVHBM , a next-generation high-bandwidth memory technology that brings higher memory performance and efficiency to XPUs. It will be validated and offered by leading memory partners, extending this advanced memory capability to NVLink Fusion customers. Traditional HBM architectures place the memory controller on the XPU die, consuming valuable silicon area that could otherwise be dedicated to compute. NVHBM, built on the same technology that NVIDIA will use for future GPUs, integrates NVIDIA’s custom memory controller into the HBM base die. By integrating the memory controller into the 3D HBM stack instead of the XPU, NVHBM delivers up to 30% greater memory bandwidth and 15% lower HBM power consumption, and frees up to 25% more area on XPU compute die compared with standard HBM4E. NVIDIA is establishing a standard NVHBM implementation, available from multiple memory providers. This reduces the engineering effort required to integrate and qualify memory across multiple suppliers — giving NVLink Fusion customers a faster path for bringing custom AI chips to market. Amazon’s Annapurna Labs will be the first to work on NVHBM as part of its broader collaboration with NVIDIA around NVLink Fusion. AWS and NVIDIA Continue NVLink Fusion Collaboration Amazo
